232.title: How the Granth is built
232.hook: 1430 pages, each called an ang, a limb: the daily banis first, then thirty-one ragas, then saloks and verses
232.howItsDone: In the gurdwara, the Guru Granth Sahib rests on a raised seat under a canopy, wrapped in cloth, with a chaur waved over it; Sikhs cite hymns by ang number, which is the same in every standard copy.

segments.voice: Yesterday, jap, and the whole Japji; your line was I actually read it, and you did. Today, a new camp, the depths, and a step back to see the whole book the Japji opens.

In the gurdwara, the Guru Granth Sahib rests on a raised seat under a canopy. It's wrapped in cloth, and someone waves a whisk over it, the way attendants once did for royalty. At night, where there's a room for it, it's carried there to rest, and in the morning it's brought out again. People bow to it when they enter. To someone new, this can look like a lot of fuss over a book. But Sikhs don't treat it as a book about the Guru. They treat it as the Guru. And that changes even the word for its pages.
screen: `A CANOPY, A WHISK, A CLOTH.` → `CARRIED TO REST AT NIGHT.` → `NOT A BOOK ABOUT THE GURU.`

segments.voice: In English you'd say page. Sikhs say ang: a limb, a part of a body. If the Granth is the living Guru, its pages aren't sheets of paper. They're limbs. The standard edition used around the world has 1430 angs, so a hymn anywhere can be found by the same number: say ang 1, and everyone who opens the Granth lands on the same place. It's built in three great sections, like a house with three floors. First, the daily banis, the hymns recited every day. Ang 1 begins with the Mool Mantar and the Japji you just finished, and the opening section ends on ang 13, with the evening hymns many Sikhs recite before sleep. Second, the heart of it: the ragas. From ang 14, with Sri Rag, the hymns are arranged by musical mode, thirty-one ragas in all, each with its own mood and time of day. Kirtan singers still follow them. Inside each raga, the Gurus' hymns come first, then the voices of the Bhagats. This section runs well past ang 1350. Third, saloks and verses of many kinds, gathered at the end. On ang 1429 comes the Mundavani, the seal, with its picture of a plate holding three things: truth, contentment and reflection. And on ang 1430, the last limb, a list of ragas.
screen: `ANG — A LIMB, NOT A PAGE.` · `THE DAILY BANIS, ANG 1 TO 13.` · `THIRTY-ONE RAGAS FROM ANG 14.` · `SALOKS AND VERSES, TO ANG 1430.` · then, large: `EVERY PAGE A LIMB.`

segments.voice: Rest one hand gently on your other arm and feel it: a limb, alive, part of you, not a tool you own. Now picture a great book open on a raised seat, each of its pages held with that same care, from ang 1, where the Mool Mantar begins, to ang 1430, where it ends. Let your hand rest there, and breathe.
Ang. A limb: the word Sikhs use for each page of the Guru Granth Sahib, 1430 of them, because the Granth is the living Guru.
Your line: every page a limb. When you hear ang, hear a body. Day two hundred thirty-two, done.

233.title: Many voices, one Guru
233.hook: it holds hymns of six Gurus, fifteen Bhagats of many backgrounds, the Bhatt poets, and a few Sikhs of the Gurus' time
233.carry: a weaver's songs beside a king's
233.howItsDone: In gurdwaras, hymns by the Bhagats such as Kabir, Farid and Ravidas are sung in kirtan and read in the daily hukamnama just as the Gurus' hymns are, all honored as gurbani.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ang, a limb; your line was every page a limb. Today, whose voices fill those limbs.

A weaver's songs sit in the same book as a king's. A Muslim mystic from the Punjab and a Hindu poet from the east sing side by side. A leatherworker, from a caste others of his time kept at a distance, even refusing to share water, has his hymns bowed to wherever the book is opened. Sixteenth-century India was divided by caste and creed in ways that decided who could learn, who could pray where, who could even be touched. Into that world, Guru Arjan put together a book, and he chose to fill it with many voices.
screen: `A WEAVER AND A KING.` → `A MYSTIC AND A POET.` → `ONE BOOK, MANY VOICES.`

segments.voice: Today's word is bani. It comes from an old word for speech, for voice. In Sikh use, bani means sacred utterance, the hymns themselves; gurbani means the Guru's word. So whose bani does the Granth hold? First, six of the Gurus: Guru Nanak, Guru Angad, Guru Amar Das, Guru Ram Das, Guru Arjan, and, added later by Guru Gobind Singh, Guru Tegh Bahadur. Second, fifteen Bhagats, devotional poets from across India, several of whom lived before Guru Nanak. Kabir, the weaver of Banaras. Sheikh Farid, a Sufi Muslim saint of the Punjab. Namdev, from a caste of tailors. Ravidas, a leatherworker. Sain, a barber. Dhanna, a farmer. Pipa, who had been a king. Jaidev, a Brahmin poet. Hindu and Muslim, high caste and low, in one book. Third, the Bhatts, bards who sang the praises of the Gurus. Fourth, a few Sikhs of the Gurus' own time, like the musicians Satta and Balwand. Guru Arjan gathered these voices when he compiled the book; tradition dates it to 1604. Just as telling is where they sit. The Bhagats' hymns aren't an appendix. They sit inside the ragas, beside the Gurus' own, and when Sikhs bow to the Guru Granth Sahib, they bow to Kabir's words and Farid's words too. All of it is honored as gurbani. The voices are many. The Guru is one.
screen: `BANI — SACRED UTTERANCE.` · `SIX GURUS.` · `FIFTEEN BHAGATS, MANY BACKGROUNDS.` · `ALL HONORED AS ONE GURU.` · then, large: `MANY VOICES, ONE GURU.`

segments.voice: Let a few voices you trust come to mind, one at a time: a grandparent, a teacher, a friend, a writer, someone from a background very different from yours. Choose one you'd want to hear more of, maybe someone you've overlooked, and hold their face in mind. Then let all the voices quiet down together, like a room settling before music begins.
Bani. Sacred utterance, the hymns of the Granth: six Gurus, fifteen Bhagats, the Bhatts and a few Sikhs of the Gurus' time, all honored as one Guru.
Your line: a weaver's songs beside a king's. Kabir and Farid, bowed to beside the Gurus. See you tomorrow.

234.title: Mahala 1, mahala 5
234.hook: every Guru signed as Nanak; the heading mahala with a number tells you which Guru
234.howItsDone: When a hymn is read in the gurdwara, the reader often announces its heading, such as Sorath mahala 5, so listeners know which Guru's words they are hearing; the hymn itself ends with the name Nanak.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bani; your line was a weaver's songs beside a king's. Today, how to tell the Gurus' voices apart, when they all use the same name.
screen: `BANI — A WEAVER'S SONGS BESIDE A KING'S.`

segments.voice: Here's a puzzle. You reach the last line of a hymn in the Granth, and it says: Nanak says this. Easy, Guru Nanak wrote it. The next hymn also ends with Nanak. And the next. But some of these hymns praise the pool of Guru Ram Das, a pool dug long after Guru Nanak was gone. They speak of things he never lived to see. So who's writing, when every one of these poets signs with the same name?
screen: `NANAK SAYS, AGAIN AND AGAIN.` → `BUT LONG AFTER HIM?` → `WHO IS WRITING?`

segments.voice: Look at the top of a hymn, not the bottom. There's a heading: first the raga, then a word and a number. Sri Rag, mahala 1. Gauri, mahala 3. Asa, mahala 5. Today's word is mahala, and the number tells you which Guru. Mahala 1 is Guru Nanak. Mahala 2, Guru Angad. Mahala 3, Guru Amar Das. Mahala 4, Guru Ram Das. Mahala 5, Guru Arjan, who compiled the book. And mahala 9, Guru Tegh Bahadur, whose hymns were added later. There's no run of mahala 10 hymns: tradition says Guru Gobind Singh added his father's hymns, then gave the Guruship to the Granth itself, and his own writings are collected elsewhere. What does mahala mean? Its meaning is debated. One common reading takes it from mahal, a house or dwelling: the first body, the fifth body. That fits the heart of it. Sikhs understand the Gurus as one light, one jot, passing from one to the next, the way one lamp lights another. The Granth itself says so, in the ballad of Satta and Balwand: the light is the same, the way is the same; only the body has changed. So when every Guru signs as Nanak, it isn't borrowing a famous name. It's saying the same light is speaking. The Bhagats, by contrast, sign with their own names: Kabir says, Ravidas says, Farid says. The bottom line tells you it's the Nanak light speaking; the heading tells you through which Guru. Now you can read the map.

segments.voice: Picture a row of oil lamps in a dark room, one of them lit. Someone tips a second lamp toward it until the wick catches, then a third from the second, then a fourth, and the same flame moves down the row. With each slow breath out, see one more lamp catch, until the room fills with light.
Mahala. The heading word with a number that tells you which Guru wrote a hymn, mahala 1 for Guru Nanak, mahala 5 for Guru Arjan, because every Guru signs as Nanak.
Your line: every guru signs as nanak. The number at the top names which one of them. That's day two hundred thirty-four.

235.title: Hukam: living in the order
235.hook: the order runs through everything; the Granth invites living in tune with it, not fighting it
235.tomorrow: Haumai: the disease with its own cure
235.howItsDone: Many Sikhs speak of accepting events as bhana, the sweet will, while still working hard and standing up for what is right; the daily hukamnama, a hymn read from the Granth each morning, takes its name from the same word, hukam.

segments.voice: Yesterday, mahala; your line was every guru signs as nanak, one light passed lamp to lamp. Today, the first of the Granth's great themes, one you met on day one of the Japji.

A few minutes before a concert, the players wander in, and the hall fills with a noisy mess of scales and scraps of melody. Then it goes quiet, and one instrument plays a single long note. Violins, cellos, horns, one by one, slide their pitch until it sits right on that note. Nobody is forced to play the same melody; each keeps its own part. But they're all in tune with one note, and that's what lets the music happen. When one violin refuses, you hear it instantly. Sikhs have a word for the note everything is tuned to.
screen: `THE ORCHESTRA TUNES UP.` → `ONE LONG NOTE.` → `EVERY PART, IN TUNE.`

segments.voice: The word is hukam. It came into Punjabi from Arabic and Persian, where it means a command, an order, a ruling. In the Granth it means the divine order running through everything: how the world is made, how it moves, how it holds together. In the very first pauri of the Japji, Guru Nanak asks how the wall of falsehood can fall, and answers: hukam rajaaee chalanaa, Nanak likhiaa naal. Walk in the will of the order; it's written with you. And in Pauri 2: hukmai andar sabh ko, baahar hukam na koe. Everyone is within the order; no one is outside it. So hukam isn't something you choose to join. You're already inside it, like every instrument in the hall. The only question is whether you play in tune, and the Granth's invitation, again and again, is to live in tune with it instead of fighting it. Fighting it looks like rage at a traffic jam, the endless replay of what should have happened, the demand that the world arrange itself around me. Living in tune means doing your part fully, then accepting what comes as part of a larger music. Sikh teachers are careful here. Living in hukam isn't sitting still while wrong is done; the same tradition honors Gurus who stood up against injustice. It's about where the fighting comes from: ego, or the order. And Pauri 2 ends with the key: whoever understands the hukam stops saying I, I, I.
screen: `HUKAM — THE ORDER IN EVERYTHING.` · `HUKAM RAJAAEE CHALANAA.` · `NO ONE IS OUTSIDE IT.` · `IN TUNE, NOT PASSIVE.` · then, large: `IN TUNE.`

segments.voice: Think of one small thing today that isn't the way you wanted, the weather, a delay, a noise outside, an ache, and notice where you've been pushing against it: your jaw, your chest, your thoughts. You don't have to like it; just stop arguing with it, and let it be exactly as it is. Breathe out and let your shoulders drop, like an instrument sliding into tune.
Hukam. The divine order running through everything. No one is outside it, and the Granth invites living in tune with it, not fighting it.
Your line: in tune. Your own part, played inside a larger music. Day two hundred thirty-five.

236.title: Haumai: the disease with its own cure
236.hook: ego is a chronic illness, says a salok of Guru Angad, and the cure lies within it too (Asa di Var, ang 466)
236.howItsDone: Asa di Var, which holds this salok, is sung in many gurdwaras in the early morning; Sikh teachers often describe haumai as the root illness that remembering the Name and living by the Guru's word are meant to heal.

segments.voice: Yesterday, hukam, the order in everything; your line was in tune. Yesterday ended with I, I, I. Today, that I.

When someone is bitten by a venomous snake, the treatment, antivenom, is made using the venom itself. A tiny, careful dose of the poison is used to teach an animal's body to fight it, and from that comes the cure. The thing that harms you becomes the way you're healed. It sounds like a riddle, but it saves lives. Guru Angad, the second Guru, wrote a short verse that works like that riddle. It names an illness, a lasting one, and then says where the medicine is hidden.
screen: `A SNAKEBITE.` → `THE CURE MADE FROM THE VENOM.` → `A RIDDLE THAT HEALS.`

segments.voice: Today's word is haumai. Say it: HAU-mai. Hau means I. Mai means me. Haumai: I-me, the self that puts itself at the center of everything. English usually says ego, but haumai is more everyday than that sounds: the voice that says my turn, my way, my hurt, my credit, all day long. You met it in the Japji: whoever understands the hukam stops saying I, I, I. Now open the Granth to ang 466, to a long hymn called Asa di Var, the ballad sung in the early morning. There, a salok of Guru Angad describes haumai like a doctor. This is its nature, he says: in haumai people act, in haumai they're bound, and they keep coming back to be born again. Then the diagnosis, in his own words: haumai deeragh rog hai. Haumai is a chronic disease. Deeragh means long, lasting; not a cold you get over in a week. And then the riddle: daaroo bhee is maahi. The medicine is in it too. Commentators read this in more than one way. Some hear that the very self that says I can turn around and say Waheguru, the same energy pointed toward the One. Others hear that the cure is found inside the person, not outside. The salok goes on: if the One shows grace, a person lives by the Guru's word, and in that discipline the pain goes. So the illness is inside, and so is the cure. You don't have to travel anywhere to find it.
screen: `HAUMAI — I-ME.` · `A CHRONIC DISEASE, SAYS GURU ANGAD.` · `DAAROO BHEE IS MAAHI.` · `THE SAME SELF, TURNED AROUND.` · then, large: `THE CURE IS INSIDE.`

segments.voice: Think back over the last day and find one me-first moment: an interruption, a need to be right, a hurt that nobody noticed you. Don't scold yourself; just see it clearly, like a doctor noticing a symptom. Then picture the same moment with the same energy turned outward, the interruption becoming listening, the need to be right becoming curiosity, and breathe with that until it settles.
Haumai. I-me: the self that puts itself at the center. Guru Angad calls it a chronic disease, and says the medicine is in it too.
Your line: the cure is inside. Haumai, the long illness, carries its own medicine. Two hundred thirty-six days in.

237.title: Naam: the Name
237.hook: Naam is more than a word; it is the presence of the One, remembered until it fills you
237.howItsDone: Many Sikhs practice naam simran by repeating Waheguru, singing kirtan, or holding the One in mind through the day; naam japo, remembering the Name, is taught alongside kirat karo, honest work, and vand chhako, sharing.

segments.voice: Yesterday, haumai, the I-me; your line was the cure is inside. Today, the medicine the Granth names most often.

A name gets said in a lot of ways. Read off a list at the dentist's office, it's flat, just a label. Shouted across a parking lot, it's a signal. And then there's the way someone who loves you says it, maybe a parent when you were small, or a grandparent who's gone now. That voice didn't only identify you. It held you. Same name, completely different thing. Said a certain way, a name carries a whole presence with it. Sikhs have a word for the Name of the One, and they mean it that second way.
screen: `A NAME READ OFF A LIST.` → `A NAME SAID WITH LOVE.` → `A NAME THAT CARRIES A PRESENCE.`

segments.voice: Today's word is naam. Literally, name. But in the Granth, naam is far more than a word for God. It's the presence of the One, running through everything, which a person can remember until it fills them. You've heard it from the very beginning. The Mool Mantar calls the One Satnam: truth is the Name. Pauri 4 of the Japji says: in the ambrosial early hours, reflect on the true Name. And Pauri 19 says it boldly: jetaa keetaa tetaa naaou. As much as has been made, that much is the Name. Vin naavai naahee ko thaaou: without the Name, there's no place at all. So naam isn't a label stuck onto creation. Creation is where the Name shows up, which is why the Granth keeps coming back to it. Sikh teaching sums up Guru Nanak's way in three simple pillars, and naam japo, remember the Name, is one of them, alongside honest work and sharing with others. Naam simran, remembering the Name, can mean repeating Waheguru, singing hymns, or simply holding the One in mind while you chop onions or drive to work. And yesterday's riddle, the disease with its own cure? Sikh teachers point to naam as that medicine. When the Name fills you, there's less room for the I-me. It isn't pushed out by force. It's more like a room filling with light: the shadows don't lose a fight; they just aren't there anymore.
screen: `NAAM — MORE THAN A LABEL.` · `SATNAM — TRUTH IS THE NAME.` · `JETAA KEETAA TETAA NAAOU.` · `THE NAME AS THE MEDICINE.` · then, large: `THE NAME FILLS YOU.`

segments.voice: No task, no counting: if you'd like, let the word Waheguru rise silently on a slow breath in, and settle on the breath out. If that word isn't yours, simply rest in the quiet, the way you'd sit in a room with someone you love without needing to talk. Let whatever presence you feel fill the space, slowly, like light.
Naam. The Name: not a label but the presence of the One, in everything that's made, remembered until it fills you.
Your line: the name fills you. Less I-me, more light in the room. Day two hundred thirty-seven, done.

238.title: Nadar: the kindly glance
238.hook: effort matters, but the Granth speaks of grace, the Beloved's glance, as what finally opens the door
238.howItsDone: Sikhs recite gur prasaad, by the Guru's grace, as the last words of the Mool Mantar, and many speak of any good outcome as coming through the Guru's kirpa, grace, while still working hard for it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, naam; your line was the name fills you. That closes a week: ang, every page a limb; bani, a weaver's songs beside a king's; mahala, every guru signs as nanak; hukam, living in tune; haumai, the cure is inside; and naam. Today, a glance.
screen: `NAAM — THE NAME FILLS YOU.` → `A WEEK: ANG, BANI, MAHALA, HUKAM, HAUMAI, NAAM.`

segments.voice: A school play. A nervous kid in the back row has rehearsed for weeks, knows every line, and still freezes when the lights come up. Then they catch a parent's eye in the audience, and the parent gives the smallest nod. That's all. And the kid breathes, and speaks. All the practice mattered. But it was the glance that opened the door.
screen: `A NERVOUS KID ON STAGE.` → `ONE GLANCE, ONE NOD.` → `THE DOOR OPENS.`

segments.voice: Today's word is nadar. It comes from the Persian nazar: sight, a look, a glance. In the Granth it means the Beloved's kindly glance: grace, given, not earned. Once you know the word, you'll find it everywhere. The Mool Mantar ends with gur prasaad: by the Guru's grace. Pauri 4 of the Japji puts it in one line: karmee aavai kaparraa, nadaree mokh duaar. By your deeds comes this garment, this life, this body. By the glance of grace comes the door of liberation. Pauri 32, where you climbed the ladder of the Name, ended: Nanak nadaree paaeeai, by grace it's reached. And the last pauri, the goldsmith's shop, closed with nadaree nadar nihaal: with a glance, the Gracious One fills them with joy. So the Granth holds two things together, and it's worth being careful here. Effort matters. The Gurus worked, served, sang, and taught others to live honestly and remember the Name. The ladder is real, and you climb it. But climbing isn't the same as arriving. The door opens by nadar. The glance isn't a reward you can demand, like a paycheck. It's more like the nod from the audience, from someone who has been watching with love all along. In the Granth's picture, you do your part, and the door is not yours to force.
screen: `NADAR — A GLANCE, FROM NAZAR.` · `NADAREE MOKH DUAAR.` · `EFFORT CLIMBS; GRACE OPENS.` · `NOT A PAYCHECK, A NOD.` · then, large: `THE GLANCE COMES.`

segments.voice: Think of one good thing in your life you didn't earn: a person who loves you, your health today, a chance someone gave you before you deserved it. Let yourself feel thankful, not for your own effort but for the gift. If you pray, thank the One for it silently, in your own way; if not, let the thanks sit warm in your chest, and breathe with it.
Nadar. The kindly glance: grace, given, not earned. Effort climbs the ladder, and in the Granth, the glance is what opens the door.
Your line: the glance comes. You do your part; the door opens by grace. A full week, closed with a glance.
